card.band: 4h. The scalar levers (histograms, predictors, filter loops, bit reader) are well known. The gain is moderate, so partial credit is dense but small. A weaker model breaks equivalence. Licence of the images needs separate checking, so generated images are used.
card.cheat: Hidden image set gives exact-byte output checks; precomputed outputs are not possible. The 0.4.1 source is not in the image.
card.grading: Hard gate: encoded bytes identical to those of the reference, and decoded pixels identical, on hidden images. Score is the median wall-clock speedup relative to the 0.4.1 speedup (NEWS claims about 25% on lossy and about 10% on lossless decode; no further detail: not found).
card.reference: Official libwebp 0.4.1, built and measured by us. The speedup is that measurement.
card.task: /app ships libwebp at 0.4.0 as a history-less snapshot with a cwebp/dwebp-style benchmark harness and image set. The agent speeds up the lossy and lossless encoder and decoder without changing the output.

facts.claim: libwebp is a real public project at github.com/webmproject/libwebp with a NEWS file
0.4.1 NEWS entry is dated 7/24/14 and claims '~25% faster lossy decode / encode (-m 4)' and '~10% faster lossless decode' (also '~5-10% faster lossless encode (-m 3/4)')

0.4.1 speedup claims are not tied to x86: the same release notes list 'AArch64 (arm64) & MIPS support/optimizations' and the release page lists 'NEON assembly additions', so the x86 speedup of 0.4.1 over 0.4.0 is not documented
Git tag v0.4.1 exists (commit 8af2771), so the 0.4.1 source is public in upstream history
0.4.0 was released 12/19/13 with only a generic 'numerous fixes, compression improvement and speed-up' line, no measured figure
Benchmark methodology, hardware and image set behind the 25%/10% figures

v1.kill_reason: Too easy and reference scale unreliable. The 0.4.1 gains are documented as ARM/MIPS NEON and AArch64 work, so the x86 reference speedup is undocumented and may be near 1. A frontier agent can recall modern byte-identical libwebp SIMD code, which would exceed the reference. Also a K5 concern: no strong, measured x86 reference is obtainable from the sources. Seal is weak because the 0.4.1 diff is public in git.

Band.why: Modern libwebp recall would beat the reference easily, so the band is too easy for a frontier model; no dated public evidence.

Build.why: Two builds and a timing harness, about 1-2 days.

Fit.why: Pure C, CPU only, fits 8 cores and 16 GB under gVisor.

Hor.why: Scope is a set of small diffs against a 0.4.0 base, not a long multi-hour job.

Lic.why: Upstream code is BSD-3 and shippable; the image licence is unchecked.

Multi.why: Several encoder and decoder paths give buckets, but each lever is small and the gain per lever is tiny.

Nov.why: Best L0 neighbour is 0.26 (S-op-011); no CROWDED overlap, though the codec subject is common.

Real.why: Real upstream project, tag and licence confirmed; the speedup claim is a one-line NEWS entry.

Ref.why: The reference is a measured 0.4.1 build, but its gain is ARM/MIPS-specific and unmeasured on x86, so the scale S-1-d is unreliable.

Seal.why: The 0.4.1 change set is public in git and modern libwebp is recallable, so the approach cannot be sealed from the agent.

Surf.why: Exact-byte checks over hidden images can scale, but the lever count is small and the grading is dominated by timing.

spike_plan.kill_if: x86 median speedup under 1.05 (reference scale degenerate), or a modern-libwebp-style SIMD recall path beats 0.4.1 by more than the claimed gain (too easy), or outputs differ between tags.
spike_plan.pass_if: Byte-identical outputs between tags on every case, and a repeatable x86 median speedup of at least 1.15 on lossy encode or decode with the variance under 5%.
steps: In a throwaway Linux container with network, fetch the v0.4.0 and v0.4.1 tags of webmproject/libwebp and build both with default flags on x86 (cmake or make).
Generate or pick 20 varied PNG/RGB images and run cwebp -m 4 (lossy) and -lossless with both builds; record encoded bytes and md5.
Run dwebp decode for lossy and lossless outputs with both builds; record pixel md5s.
Time 10 repeats per case per build with taskset pinned to one core; compute median speedup 0.4.0 -> 0.4.1 on x86.
Check whether any x86 code path changed between the tags (diff src/dsp for SSE2 files) to explain the result.

v1.summary: The 0.4.0 to 0.4.1 libwebp speedup is real but documented only as one-line NEWS claims that point at ARM/MIPS NEON work, so there is no evidence of an x86 gain to score against. A frontier agent can recall far faster modern libwebp, so the task is killed as too easy (K8), with a weak reference scale as a second concern.
